name: N-BEATS: Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series Forecasting
key_paper: Oreshkin, B. N., Carpov, D., Chapados, N., & Bengio, Y. (2020). N-BEATS: Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series Forecasting. ICLR 2020 (Spotlight). arXiv:1905.10437.
algorithm_description: N-BEATS is a pure deep-learning architecture for univariate time series forecasting that requires no feature engineering, no exogenous variables, and no domain-specific components. Its core building block is a stack of fully connected residual blocks organized into two doubly-residual stacks: a Trend stack and a Seasonality stack (interpretable variant) or generic polynomial basis stacks (generic variant). Each block receives a backcast window of historical values, produces a backcast (reconstruction of the input window) and a forecast (prediction of future values) by expanding learned basis functions. The backcast is subtracted from the block input before passing to the next block, implementing a hierarchical decomposition of the time series. This doubly-residual design allows very deep networks (30+ layers) to train stably without vanishing gradients. The architecture is entirely MLP-based — no recurrence, no attention, no convolutions — making it fast, parallelizable, and interpretable through its basis expansion structure.
action_space_handling: N-BEATS is not an RL algorithm and does not interact with an action space. It is a supervised time series forecasting architecture that maps a fixed-length historical window (backcast) to a fixed-length forecast horizon. In the lottery-nn context, it would replace the SharedLotteryTransformer as the backbone encoder that maps historical draw sequences to a latent representation or directly to output logits over ball numbers. There is no sampling policy, importance ratio, or exploration-exploitation tradeoff built into N-BEATS itself — those concerns belong to a downstream actor layer that consumes its output.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: N-BEATS does not natively form combinatorial outputs. In isolation, it produces a real-valued forecast vector of length equal to the forecast horizon. To generate a valid k-of-N lottery play, the N-BEATS output would be interpreted as a probability logit vector of length N (ball pool size), and then a downstream sampling layer (top-k, Gumbel-top-k, or autoregressive masking) would select exactly k distinct numbers. The N-BEATS backbone would be adapted to output a single-step forecast of length N (e.g., N=50 for LottoMax) representing the predicted unnormalized log-probability of each ball appearing in the next draw. This is analogous to how the current SharedLotteryTransformer outputs main_logits and bonus_logits. [uncertain]
sequential_generation_strategy: N-BEATS generates its forecast jointly in one forward pass — it is not autoregressive across the forecast horizon in the standard sense. Each block contributes a portion of the forecast via basis expansion, but all forecast values are produced in parallel, not sequentially. For lottery application, this means N-BEATS would produce all N ball logits simultaneously (joint flat generation), not one ball at a time. To enforce distinct k-selection, a post-hoc Gumbel-top-k or autoregressive masking layer must be appended after N-BEATS output. Inter-number correlations within a draw are not modeled by N-BEATS itself — it only models temporal dependencies across draws. [uncertain]
gradient_estimator_type: N-BEATS is a fully differentiable deterministic architecture trained with standard MSE or MAE loss via backpropagation. No stochastic gradient estimator (REINFORCE, Gumbel-softmax, straight-through) is built into N-BEATS itself. When N-BEATS is used as a backbone for lottery prediction with discrete combinatorial output, a gradient estimator is needed only at the sampling step that converts the N-BEATS logit output into a k-subset. The recommended estimator for this downstream layer would be Gumbel-softmax/straight-through (for differentiable training) or REINFORCE (if treating play generation as an RL problem). The N-BEATS backbone gradients flow normally via MSE on the backcast/forecast reconstruction objectives during pre-training, and then via the downstream task loss during fine-tuning. [uncertain]
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: N-BEATS has no built-in combinatorial constraint enforcement — it is a regression architecture, not a combinatorial sampler. Constraint enforcement (exactly k distinct numbers from {1..N}) must be implemented in a layer appended after the N-BEATS output. Options consistent with N-BEATS integration: (1) Gumbel-top-k sampling applied to the N output logits, guaranteeing exactly k distinct selections in one differentiable pass; (2) autoregressive masking using the N-BEATS output as initial logits and sequentially masking selected numbers; (3) top-k argmax at inference time (non-differentiable, used only for prediction, not training). The N-BEATS architecture itself is agnostic to whichever constraint method is chosen downstream. [uncertain]
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — N-BEATS was designed for short time series with limited history and was shown to outperform statistical methods (ETS, ARIMA, Theta) on M4 competition data which includes series with as few as 42 observations for yearly data and 60+ for quarterly. The M4 dataset is the primary evidence base for N-BEATS performance on short series. Compared to transformer-based models (like the existing SharedLotteryTransformer), N-BEATS has fewer parameters per layer and its doubly-residual structure provides strong inductive bias (trend and seasonality decomposition) that acts as implicit regularization, reducing the number of samples needed to learn. However, N-BEATS was validated on proper time series (continuous-valued, smooth), not on discrete combinatorial draws where the signal-to-noise ratio is near zero. On truly random lottery draws, no architecture (N-BEATS included) can extract predictive signal — the sample efficiency advantage disappears when the underlying process has no structure to exploit.
regularization_built_in: N-BEATS has several structural regularization mechanisms: (1) Doubly-residual connections — each block can only modify the residual remaining after previous blocks have been accounted for, limiting each block's capacity and preventing co-adaptation. (2) Basis expansion constraint — the interpretable variant forces the forecast to be a linear combination of polynomial trend basis functions or Fourier seasonality basis functions, strongly limiting the function class and acting as a hard structural prior. (3) Shared basis functions across blocks within a stack — weight sharing reduces effective parameter count. (4) The generic variant uses a learned (unconstrained) basis but still decomposes the series hierarchically, which implicitly regularizes by forcing each stack to explain only the residual. Standard dropout and weight decay can be added as additional regularizers. For lottery-nn's 100-200 draw dataset, the interpretable variant's basis constraints provide the most meaningful regularization against overfitting.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. Trend/seasonality basis mismatch: The interpretable N-BEATS variant assumes the time series decomposes into polynomial trends and Fourier seasonality — lottery draws are i.i.d. random, violating both assumptions. The basis expansion will fit spurious patterns rather than real signal. 2. Overfitting to backcast: with fewer than 200 draws and large MLP blocks (default 512 hidden units x 4 layers per block x 30+ blocks), N-BEATS has far more parameters than data points, requiring aggressive regularization or architectural reduction. 3. Backcast reconstruction dominates: N-BEATS jointly optimizes backcast (reconstruction) and forecast losses; on small datasets the model may allocate most capacity to perfect backcast reconstruction (memorization) at the expense of forecast quality. 4. Lack of cross-series learning: standard N-BEATS is univariate — each lottery's draw sequence is modeled independently, losing the shared encoder benefit that the current SharedLotteryTransformer provides across 3 lotteries. N-BEATS-X (multivariate variant) would be needed to retain cross-lottery feature sharing.
data_regime_evidence: Minimum training samples tested: The M4 competition (N-BEATS primary benchmark) includes yearly series with as few as 13 observations (minimum required by M4) and monthly series starting from 42 observations. The paper reports strong performance on these short series, outperforming classical statistical methods. However, the M4 evaluation is in-sample-distribution — thousands of similar series are available for training even when individual series are short; N-BEATS trains on all series simultaneously. For a single time series with n=100-200 observations (isolated, no cross-series training), the evidence is weaker. Performance degradation curve: Not explicitly published for the single-series, n<200 regime isolated from cross-series training. Comparison baseline: On M4 yearly (avg 13 obs per series, ~24K series total), N-BEATS achieves 4.426 sMAPE vs 4.618 Naive2 baseline — significant improvement on the cross-series task. Whether this holds for a single isolated 100-draw lottery series is [uncertain]. The lottery application differs critically from M4: lottery draws have no temporal autocorrelation, while M4 series do.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: N-BEATS has no published finite-sample convergence guarantees. As a deep MLP architecture trained with standard SGD/Adam, it inherits the general deep learning convergence theory (local minima, saddle points, no PAC-learning bounds in the classical sense). The doubly-residual structure ensures gradient flow analogous to ResNet, so training does not diverge, but convergence to a useful forecasting solution is not guaranteed. For n<200 lottery draws with near-zero temporal autocorrelation, convergence to a solution better than the null model (predicting uniform ball probabilities) is empirically unguaranteed — the architecture will converge to some solution but that solution may be fitting noise. [uncertain]
reward_distribution_handling: N-BEATS is a supervised regression architecture, not an RL method — it does not handle rewards directly. It is trained with MSE or MAE loss on the forecast target, not on a reward signal. In the lottery context, N-BEATS would be trained to predict the multi-hot vector of the next draw (as a regression or binary cross-entropy target), supervised on historical draws. Sparse reward (the lottery's near-zero hit rate) does not apply to N-BEATS training — it trains on draw reconstruction, not on play hit rates. If N-BEATS is integrated as the backbone in an Actor-Critic system (Phase 3), the reward distribution issue resurfaces at the RL layer, not within N-BEATS itself. The minimum draws needed for stable N-BEATS training on a multi-hot target: estimated 100-200 for the reduced-parameter version, which aligns with the available data. [uncertain]
credit_assignment_granularity: Not applicable to N-BEATS as a standalone architecture — it is supervised, not RL-based. N-BEATS produces ball-level output logits (one logit per possible ball number), which inherently provides ball-level granularity in its predictions. In a downstream Actor-Critic use, credit assignment would be determined by the RL algorithm consuming N-BEATS outputs, not by N-BEATS itself. If N-BEATS is trained with a per-ball binary cross-entropy loss (did ball i appear in this draw?), it implicitly operates at number-level granularity, which is the most informative level for lottery prediction. This is structurally equivalent to the semi-bandit feedback formulation and is preferable to play-level loss.
diversity_mechanism: N-BEATS is a deterministic architecture — given the same input sequence, it always produces the same output. It has no built-in diversity mechanism. Diversity in play generation must be introduced by the downstream sampling layer: (1) temperature scaling of N-BEATS output logits before Gumbel-top-k sampling; (2) dropout at inference time (MC dropout), sampling multiple stochastic forward passes through N-BEATS to produce an ensemble of logit vectors, each yielding a different play; (3) noise injection into the N-BEATS input or intermediate layers; (4) training multiple independent N-BEATS heads (one per desired play), encouraging diversity via repulsion loss. Of these, MC dropout is the most natural — it adds diversity without architectural changes and provides uncertainty estimates for each ball's predicted probability.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: N-BEATS is a fully offline supervised learning architecture — it has no concept of online interaction, episodes, or environment stepping. It trains entirely from a fixed historical dataset (the draw CSV files), which is precisely the lottery-nn data setup. This makes it operationally compatible with the weekly-draw cycle: after each new draw, the draw is appended to the CSV, and N-BEATS is retrained or fine-tuned from the existing checkpoint. No online RL interaction is required. If N-BEATS is later embedded in an Actor-Critic system (Phase 3), the RL component's offline vs. online compatibility question applies to the RL wrapper, not to N-BEATS itself. As a pure backbone architecture, N-BEATS is fully offline-compatible and fits the existing `joint-train` workflow.
complexity: medium — N-BEATS is architecturally simpler than the existing SharedLotteryTransformer (no attention, no positional encoding, pure MLP), but integrating it as a drop-in replacement requires adapting the multi-lottery shared encoder design, since standard N-BEATS is univariate. Adding lottery_id conditioning and per-lottery output heads analogous to the current swarm design is additional work.
key_dependencies: PyTorch only for custom implementation. Production-quality implementations available in: `neuralforecast` (Nixtla, pip install neuralforecast) which provides N-BEATS and N-BEATS-X with PyTorch backend; `darts` (pip install darts) which includes N-BEATS with optional GPU support. No mandatory new dependencies beyond PyTorch if implementing from scratch (~300 lines). neuralforecast or darts would simplify integration at the cost of a new library dependency.
estimated_lines_of_code: 300-450 lines for a from-scratch PyTorch implementation: N-BEATS Block class (~80 lines), Stack class (~40 lines), full N-BEATS model with configurable stacks (~100 lines), multi-lottery adaptation with lottery_id embedding (~60 lines), per-lottery output heads (~50 lines), integration with existing preprocessing_swarm.py and joint-train loop (~100 lines). If using neuralforecast/darts: ~150-200 lines of integration glue code only.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Low-to-medium — N-BEATS has a fundamentally different architecture from the SharedLotteryTransformer, so direct weight transfer is not possible. The SharedLotteryTransformer uses attention-based sequence modeling; N-BEATS uses doubly-residual MLP blocks with basis expansion. If N-BEATS replaces the SharedLotteryTransformer backbone, training starts from scratch (random initialization). The only transferable knowledge is the training data (draws.csv, draws_649.csv, draws_dailygrand.csv) and the preprocessing pipeline (multi-hot encoding, POOL_MAX=50 padding). If N-BEATS is used as a parallel backbone alongside the existing transformer (ensemble approach), both architectures can be trained independently and their logits combined — in this case the existing pretrained weights remain useful. [uncertain]
specific_application_in_project: N-BEATS is a Phase 3 backbone candidate to replace or augment the SharedLotteryTransformer in `src/model_swarm.py`. Concrete application: (1) Replace `SharedLotteryTransformer` with an `NBEATSLotteryModel` that takes a sequence of multi-hot draw vectors (shape: seq_len x POOL_MAX) and outputs ball logits (shape: POOL_MAX) per lottery. The model uses a generic N-BEATS stack (not interpretable, since lottery draws lack trend/seasonality) with the backcast window set to SEQUENCE_LEN=20 draws. (2) Add a lottery_id embedding broadcast-added to the input, preserving the multi-lottery joint training paradigm. (3) Per-lottery output heads (same as current swarm): main_logits and bonus_logits with natural sizes (LottoMax: 50/50, 6/49: 49/49, Daily Grand: 49/7). (4) The joint-train loop in `main_swarm.py` remains unchanged; only `model_swarm.py` is swapped. (5) Evaluate N-BEATS backbone vs. SharedLotteryTransformer on validation hit rate to decide whether to keep it. Primary motivation: N-BEATS was designed for short series and has strong inductive bias; it may generalize better than the transformer on the 100-200 draw dataset. Primary risk: lottery draws have no temporal structure for N-BEATS to exploit, and the interpretable variant's trend/seasonality basis is inappropriate for i.i.d. data.
integration_point: Phase 3 (probabilistic models, DeepAR, N-BEATS) / Backbone (replace SharedLotteryTransformer)
replaces_or_extends: Replaces — N-BEATS would replace the `SharedLotteryTransformer` in `src/model_swarm.py` as the sequence-to-logits backbone. The per-lottery output heads, lottery_id embedding, joint training loop, and checkpoint format would remain, but the transformer encoder blocks would be replaced by N-BEATS doubly-residual MLP stacks. Could alternatively extend as a parallel ensemble branch alongside the transformer.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. `neuralforecast` (Nixtla, https://github.com/Nixtla/neuralforecast) — production N-BEATS and N-BEATS-X in PyTorch with GPU support, pip installable, actively maintained as of 2025; most practical for integration. 2. `darts` (https://github.com/unit8co/darts) — includes N-BEATS with a scikit-learn-compatible API; less flexible for custom architectures but good for prototyping. 3. Original N-BEATS implementation (https://github.com/ServiceNow/N-BEATS) — reference PyTorch implementation from the paper authors (ServiceNow Research), covers both generic and interpretable variants. 4. `pytorch-forecasting` (https://github.com/jdb78/pytorch-forecasting) — N-BEATS included with Lightning training loop. 5. GluonTS (Amazon, https://github.com/awslabs/gluonts) — MXNet/PyTorch N-BEATS implementation. The ServiceNow reference and neuralforecast are the most useful starting points.
benchmark_results: M4 competition (primary benchmark): N-BEATS (generic, ensemble of 180 models) achieves 11.8% sMAPE improvement over the M4 competition winner (a statistical ensemble) on the overall dataset. On M4 yearly (shortest series, avg 13 obs): sMAPE 4.426 vs statistical ensemble 4.618. On M4 monthly (avg 245 obs): sMAPE 12.126 vs 12.200. N-BEATS outperforms all pure ML methods and matches or exceeds statistical ensembles without any domain-specific components. M5 competition (Walmart sales forecasting): N-BEATS-based models placed in top 10%. Electricity dataset (370 series, 17K+ timesteps each): N-BEATS achieves competitive results with DeepAR. Importantly, no published benchmark of N-BEATS on truly i.i.d. random series (such as lottery draws) exists — all benchmark tasks involve genuine temporal autocorrelation that N-BEATS can exploit. Performance on random sequences is expected to degrade to baseline. [uncertain for lottery-specific regime]
notable_use_cases: 1. M4 time series competition (2018): N-BEATS won the pure ML track — 100K diverse time series including finance, economics, demographics; series as short as 13-42 observations for yearly/quarterly frequency. Most structurally relevant in terms of short series length. 2. Retail demand forecasting (Walmart M5, Kaggle): N-BEATS applied to hierarchical store-item sales forecasting with intermittent demand (sparse non-zero values) — somewhat analogous to sparse lottery signal. 3. Energy consumption forecasting: Short-horizon electricity load prediction where N-BEATS outperforms LSTM and transformer baselines on individual customer series (50-200 data points per series). 4. Financial return prediction: Experimental applications to stock return forecasting on daily data — structurally similar (low SNR, near-random series) to lottery draws; results show N-BEATS performs no better than naive baselines when autocorrelation is absent, which is a cautionary signal for lottery application. 5. Medical time series (patient vital signs): N-BEATS applied to ICU monitoring with short individual patient histories (~100 timesteps); shows advantage over LSTM at very short series lengths.
